div.p: The group-based preemptive scheduling provides a flexible mechanism to define the preemptive relations between tasks. However, this scheduling scheme together with a resource access synchronization protocol and requirements of fault tolerance makes the predication of a real-time system's behaviors more difficult than traditional scheduling scheme. The major contribution of our work is an algorithm to calculate the worst-case response time for tasks under the fault-tolerant group-based preemptive scheduling. We first present the algorithm assuming that no task suffers any error. Then the algorithm is extended to consider a fault model and a primary/alternative fault-tolerant mechanism. Based on the tasks' worst-case response time, the schedulability of a given task set can be determined. Moreover, we also introduce a method to calculate the minimum allowed time between two consecutive faults.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Some real-time operating systems allow tasks to combine aspects of preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling. The definition of a non-preemptable task makes sense in a full preemptive operating system in the case: The execution time of the task is in the same magnitude of the time of a task switch, RAM is to be used economically to provide space for saving the task context, or the task can not be preempted. To provide a flexible mechanism defining the preemptive relations between tasks in an application, a group-based preemptive scheduling scheme can be adopted. In this scheme, tasks can be put into groups. Within a group, tasks behave like non-preemptable tasks, i.e. they are not allowed to be preempted by tasks with higher priorities in the same group. For tasks with a priority higher than the highest priority within the group, all the tasks within the group can be preempted by them. Besides providing the flexibility of mixing preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling, the group-based preemptive scheduling also provides a means to control resource access. Within a group, tasks execute serially, there is no conflict of access to the shared resource. One can define inter-task invariants on the shared state and be assured that, while the present task is running, no other tasks can violate the invariants. A representative application of group-based preemptive scheduling is the OSEK/VXD OS [1], which is an industry standard for an open-ended architecture for distributed control units in vehicles. In this standard, internal resources are used to implement the group mechanism.

The ability to tolerate faults becomes a more critical characteristic for hard real-time systems, in which the missing of time requirements can result in catastrophic results. Systems with requirements of reliability are traditionally built in some level of replication or redundancy to maintain the properties of correctness and timeliness even in the case of faults. Faults can be tolerated by using hardware, software, information and time redundancy. In certain classes of applications, it may not be feasible to provide hardware redundancy due to space, weight and cost considerations. Such systems need to exploit software, information and time redundancy techniques, especially the combination of these techniques.

However, the implementation of such systems increases the complexity of keeping the system computation complying with the requirements specification. Effective schedulability analysis, which takes the fault model, fault tolerance mechanisms and the scheduling algorithm into consideration, is needed to guarantee the timeliness property.

In this paper, we focus on the schedulability analysis for fault-tolerant group-based preemptive scheduling model. The schedulability analysis is based on the calculation of the worst-case response times of tasks in a fixed priority task set. We first propose an algorithm to calculate the worst-case response time of tasks without fault-tolerant mechanism. The algorithm is then extended to deal with the effects of a fault model and fault-tolerant mechanism. According to their worst-case response time, if all the tasks of a given task set can be completed before their deadlines, the task set is schedulable.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. The next section briefly surveys related work. Section 3 presents the computation model used in this paper. Section 4 proposes the schedulability analysis algorithm for group-based task scheduling without fault-tolerance mechanism. After that, an extended algorithm considering the effects of our fault model and fault-tolerant mechanism is presented in Section 5. In the same section we also introduce a method to calculate the allowed maximum fault's rate. Finally we conclude our work in Section 6.

div.head: RELATED WORK
div.p: Research on schedulability analysis for fixed priority scheduling can be split to two classes. One class of techniques is based on utilization bound U which allows a simple test of the form i U U ≤ ∑ to determine a task set's schedulability [2], [3]. For example, in Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS) [2], U = n(2 1/n -1), where n is the total number of tasks. These methods have low overheads and adapt to online schedulability test. The shortcoming of them is their pessimism since some schedulable task sets may have higher utilizations than the bound U. The other class of techniques is based on the response time analysis techniques, which can provide exact schedulability analysis [4], [5], [6]. Such techniques have been increasingly developed for less restrictive computational models, thus allowing tasks to interact via shared resources, to have deadlines less than their periods [4], release jitter [4] and deadlines greater than their periods [7]. Furthermore, these methods can also be used in distributed real-time systems [8]. Compared with the methods based on utilization bound, response time analysis has higher overhead, so it is usually used as off-line test.

There are few papers which specifically deal with exact time and scheduling issues in fault-tolerant systems based on response time analysis. A study done by Burns, Davis and Punnekkat [5] provides schedulability tests for fault tolerant task sets scheduled with full preemptive priority algorithm. The recovery of tasks is modeled as alternative tasks that should be executed to recover the system from an erroneous state. The authors have shown that fault-tolerance based on error-recovery techniques can be easily modeled by response time analysis. The response time analysis of [4] is extended to implement this fault tolerance approach. Fixed point recursive computations are used to determine the response time of each task if a fault occurs during its execution.

Based on the work of [5], Lima and Burns [6] also studied the approach to run the recovery of tasks with higher priorities and provided an effective schedulability test to guarantee the predictability of system with this character.

The methods used in [5] and [6] are much like that we used in this paper. However, both of them assume a full preemptive priority scheduling model. Their calculation of a task's response time is tightly based on this assumption and must consider the effects of other ready tasks in the task set. In the group-based preemptive scheduling, the flexible preemptive relations between tasks make the analysis of the effects from other ready tasks much more complex. Besides, [5] and [6] do not study the effects of the resource access synchronization protocol in detail, which is a very critical issue in real-time operating systems and will deeply affect the accuracy of a time analyzing algorithm. We need a new method to accurately evaluate the effects of various factors and calculate the response time of a task under the groupbased preemptive scheduling.

div.head: COMPUTATION MODEL
div.p: In this paper we only consider uniprocessor systems. We assume that there is a set Γ = {τ 1 ,…,τ n } of n tasks, called primary tasks, that must be scheduled by the system without any errors. Any primary task τ i in Γ has a period, T i , a deadline D i (D i ≤ T i ), and a worst-case computation time, C i . Tasks can be periodic or sporadic. For sporadic tasks, the period means the minimum inter-arrival time. Each primary task τ i can have some alternative tasks associated with it. Each alternative task corresponds to a given action taken to recover τ i from a given error. Any alternative task has a worst-case computation time, also called worst-case recovery time. To simplify the task model, we assume that all alternative tasks associated with τ i run at the same priority level as τ i . Hence, we do not include the details of individual alternative task per primary hereafter in the description. We only need to refer to the alternative task with the longest worst-case recovery time in case of errors in task τ i . We use a i to denote this alternative task and Ca i to denote its worst-case recovery time.

Primary tasks are dynamically scheduled according to some fixed priority assignment algorithm (e.g. deadline monotonic), which attributes a distinct priority to each task τ i in Γ. We consider n different priority levels (1, 2,…, n), where τ i has a higher priority than τ i+1 . The alternative task of τ i is assumed to execute at the same priority level as that of τ i . For the simplicity of notation we define three subsets of Γ: hp(i) represents the tasks whose priorities are greater than τ i 's priority, hpe(i) denotes those tasks whose priorities are greater than or equal to τ i 's priority, and lp(i) presents the tasks whose priorities are lower than τ i 's priority. To avoid the problems of priority inversion and deadlocks caused by resource access conflicts, we assume the priority ceiling protocol [9] is used.

Based on the above assumptions, we define a group as a set of primary tasks, which cover a certain range of priorities. Tasks within the group behave like non-preemptable tasks. The priorities of tasks within the same group must be consecutive, which is to say that if a task does not belong to a group, it must have a priority higher or lower than that of all the tasks in the group, and it can preempt all of tasks within that group or be preempted by them.

We assume that any alternative task belongs to the same group with its primary task. Therefore, the alternative task has the same priority and preemption property with its primary task. We assume that errors are detected in the task level. When an error interrupts the execution of a task, the system must schedule an appropriate alternative task, which is responsible for carrying out the error-processing procedure and has to finish before the deadline of its primary task. If other errors take place in the alternative tasks, we assume that it is scheduled again for re-execution. We also assume that there is no cost associated with any scheduling of primary or alternative tasks. Further, we assume that all errors are detected by the system and faults only affect the results produced by the executing task.
The kinds of fault with which we are dealing are those that can be treated in the task level, for example, design faults.

It may be possible to use techniques such as exception handling or recovery blocks to perform appropriate recovery actions [5], modeled here as alternative tasks. In addition, some kind of transient faults can also be recovered through either the re-execution of the faulty task or the execution of some compensation actions. Please notice that more severe kinds of fault such as hardware damage and the scheduler failure cannot be treated in the task level. Tolerating these kinds of faults requires spatial redundancy, which is not covered in this paper. We assume that in the analysis there is a minimum time between two consecutive error occurrences, T F . In practice, it's important for application designers to determine the value of T F for a given task set. We will give a method to calculate T F in section 5.

div.head: SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS FOR GROUP-BASED PREEMPTIVE SCHEDULING
div.p: In this section, we will discuss the schedulability problem for the group-based preemptive scheduling considering that no task suffers any error. The schedulability of a task set can be determined by comparing the tasks' worst-case response times with their deadlines. Therefore, the core issue is to determine the worst-case response time, R i , of each task in the task set. According to [4], R i can be expressed as:

where C i is the worst-case execution time (WCET) of task i, B i is the blocking factor of task τ i (a bound on the time that a lower priority task can execute and prevent the execution of task τ i ) and I i is the worst-case preemption time from higher priority tasks and is called interference time. The WCET of a task can be determined by testing or analyzing task codes, which is not covered in this paper. We assume the WCETs of all the tasks in Γ are available. In the rest portion of this section, we will discuss how to calculate B i and I i for a given task τ i and derivate the method to compute its worst-case response time R i .

div.head: Blocking Time
div.p: The tasks with lower priority may block the execution of τ i in two ways. One type of delay is caused by resources access synchronization. If τ i requires a certain resource in its execution, it has to wait for a running lower priority task to release the resources before τ i can obtain the resource and start to execute. The delay time depends on the resource access synchronization mechanism. In this paper, we assume the priority ceiling protocol [9] is adopted to synchronize resource access between tasks. According to this protocol, the ceiling priority will be set at least to the highest priority of all tasks that access a resource. The ceiling priority must be lower than the lowest priority of all tasks that do not access the resource, and which have priorities higher than the highest priority of all tasks that access the resource. If a task requires a resource, and its current priority is lower than the ceiling priority of the resource, the priority of the task will be raised to the ceiling priority of the resource. If the task releases the resource, the priority of this task will be reset to the priority which was assigned before requiring that resource. Priority ceiling results in a possible time delay for tasks with priorities equal to or below the resource priority. div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we proposed an algorithm to calculate the worst-case response time of fixed priority tasks under the group-based preemptive scheduling model. The resource access synchronization is also involved in this algorithm by examining the blocking time incurred by the priority ceiling protocol. Then the algorithm is extended to deal with the effects from the fault model and the primary/alterative faulttolerant mechanism. Based on the worst-case response time of all the tasks, the schedulability of a given task set can be determined. Moreover, we also introduced a method to calculate the minimum allowed time between two consecutive faults. Both of the algorithms can be easily implemented and applied in the design step of practical real-time systems. Our program of further work includes studying the schedulability analysis technology in distributed fault-tolerant real-time control systems, which is more complex and wildly deployed in safety-critical applications.
